description: In the Odyssey, Odysseus faces the Cyclops Polyphemus. His [[metis]] saves him, but his pride draws down the anger of Poseidon.

hero.hook: A one eyed giant is eating his men. Odysseus cannot win by force. So he invents a name: Nobody.

blocks.text: After the Trojan War, **Odysseus**, king of the island of Ithaca, tried to get home. Homer tells the story of his voyage in the **Odyssey**. In Book IX, he lands on a fertile island where the [[Cyclopes]] live, solitary giants with a single eye.

There he met **Polyphemus**, son of the sea god **Poseidon**. The episode is not just a monster story. It is a lesson: [[metis]], cunning intelligence, can beat brute force. But [[hubris]], overreaching pride, can ruin everything.

Odysseus landed with twelve companions. The Cyclopes have no assemblies, no laws, no real farming. They live in caves. The Greeks, by contrast, believed in [[xenia]]: the sacred duty to welcome a stranger, under the protection of Zeus.

blocks.caption: Polyphemus the Cyclops, force without law

blocks.text: Inside the cave the men found cheeses and livestock. His companions wanted to leave. Odysseus insisted on waiting for the owner, hoping for a guest gift. A mistake. Polyphemus came back, sealed the entrance with a huge rock, and ate two of the Greeks. Force would not be enough. They had to be clever.

Odysseus cut a stake from an olive trunk, a wood dear to Athena, goddess of wisdom. He hid it. Then he offered Polyphemus a very strong wine, barely watered. The giant got drunk. Before falling asleep, he asked his guest for his name.
In Greek, Odysseus says his name is **Outis**, “Nobody.” The word also echoes **metis**, cunning. Homer plays on the double meaning: it really is cunning that defeats the giant.

blocks.caption: Odysseus and his men blind Polyphemus, a famous scene on Greek vases

blocks.text: Odysseus answered: “My name is **Nobody**.” Then his men drove the burning stake into the single eye. The other Cyclopes came running. “Who is killing you?” they shouted. “Nobody!” answered Polyphemus. They walked away, thinking of some divine illness.

The next morning the blinded Polyphemus guarded the exit. He ran his hands over the back of every sheep. Odysseus tied his companions under the bellies of the woolliest animals. He hung himself under the biggest ram. The giant stroked the animal without feeling the enemy just below.

Once at sea, Odysseus could not hold back. He shouted his real name, his lineage, his city. He wanted [[kleos]], the glory that survives through a name. Polyphemus could at last curse a precise target before his father Poseidon.

Polyphemus prayed to Poseidon: let Odysseus never reach home, or reach it late, alone, after losing every one of his companions. That curse shapes the ten years of wandering that follow. The sea becomes a punishment.

blocks.caption: Poseidon, god of the sea, avenges his son Polyphemus

blocks.text: The myth sets two kinds of heroism against each other. In the Iliad, you win by strength and fame. In the Odyssey, you survive by holding back. Odysseus won with his mind. He lost through the pride of wanting to be recognized.
Against Polyphemus, Odysseus won through [[metis]] and the name “Nobody.” By revealing his identity for [[kleos]], he set off the anger of Poseidon and stretched out his exile.

sections.title: The curse that sets the Odyssey in motion
